title: Baking soda volcano
steps: 1. Place the bottle inside a tray, to catch any overflow.
2. Pour 2 spoons of baking soda into the bottle.
3. Add a few drops of food coloring, if you like.
4. Slowly pour vinegar into the bottle and watch the foam come out.
whyItWorks: Baking soda (a base) reacts with vinegar (an acid) and releases carbon dioxide gas, which forms the foam.
imageAlt: Foam coming out of a container with baking soda and vinegar

title: Oil and water layers
steps: 1. Fill half of a clear cup with water.
2. Add food coloring to the water and stir.
3. Slowly pour vegetable oil on top of the water.
4. Watch the two layers form without mixing.
whyItWorks: Oil is less dense than water and does not mix with it, so it floats on top in a separate layer.
imageAlt: Layers of oil and colored water that do not mix in a cup

title: Dancing raisins
steps: 1. Fill a clear cup with sparkling water.
2. Drop 5 to 6 raisins into the cup.
3. Watch the raisins rise and sink on their own.
whyItWorks: Gas bubbles stick to the raisins and make them float; when the bubbles pop at the surface, the raisins sink again.

title: Walking rainbow
steps: 1. Set up 3 cups with colored water (a different color in each) and 3 empty cups, alternating in a row.
2. Fold paper towel strips and put one end in a full cup and the other end in the empty cup next to it.
3. Wait and watch the water "walk" along the paper towel to the empty cups.
4. Watch the colors mix and create new colors in the middle cups.
whyItWorks: The paper absorbs the water through capillary action, pulling it upward along the fibers until it reaches the empty cup.

title: Color explosion in milk
steps: 1. Pour milk into a shallow bowl, enough to cover the bottom.
2. Add several drops of different food coloring on the surface of the milk.
3. Dip the tip of a cotton swab in dish soap.
4. Touch the swab to the middle of the colored drops and watch the color explosion.
whyItWorks: The soap breaks up the fat in the milk and spreads quickly across the surface, pushing the coloring and creating swirls of color.
imageAlt: Colors spreading in a bowl of milk with dish soap

title: Sugar crystals on a string
steps: 1. Ask an adult to heat water and dissolve lots of sugar into it, until no more will dissolve.
2. Let the water cool a little and pour it into a cup.
3. Tie a cotton string to a pencil and rest the pencil across the cup, with the string in the liquid.
4. Wait a few days and watch crystals grow on the string.
whyItWorks: As the water cools and evaporates, it can no longer hold as much dissolved sugar, and the extra sugar forms solid crystals on the string.
imageAlt: Sugar crystals grown on a string

title: Invisible lemon ink
steps: 1. Squeeze a little lemon juice into a small bowl.
2. Use a cotton swab to write or draw something on the paper with the lemon juice.
3. Let it dry completely, until it becomes invisible.
4. Ask an adult to hold the paper close to (without touching) a warm, lit lightbulb until the message turns brown.
whyItWorks: Lemon juice weakens the paper; when warmed, those parts turn brown faster than the rest, revealing the drawing.

title: Homemade lava lamp
steps: 1. Fill a quarter of the bottle with water and the rest with vegetable oil.
2. Add a few drops of food coloring.
3. Break an effervescent tablet into pieces and drop one piece into the bottle.
4. Watch the colorful bubbles rise and fall.
whyItWorks: The tablet reacts with the water and releases gas, which rises through the oil carrying bubbles of colored water; when the gas escapes, the bubbles sink again.
imageAlt: Colorful bubbles rising in a bottle of oil and water

title: Static balloon and water
steps: 1. Blow up the balloon and tie it closed.
2. Rub the balloon on your dry hair or a wool cloth for about 20 seconds.
3. Turn on the tap until a thin stream of water flows.
4. Bring the balloon close to the water stream, without touching it, and watch what happens.
whyItWorks: Rubbing the balloon charges it with static electricity, which attracts the water molecules and makes the water stream bend toward the balloon.
imageAlt: A balloon bending a thin stream of water from a tap

title: Egg floating in salt water
steps: 1. Fill one cup with plain tap water.
2. Fill another cup with water and stir in several spoons of salt until dissolved.
3. Carefully place one egg in each cup.
4. Watch: the egg sinks in the plain water, but floats in the salt water.
whyItWorks: Salt water is denser than plain water, so it can push the egg upward and make it float.
imageAlt: One egg floating in a cup of salt water and another sunk in a cup of plain water

title: Naked egg in vinegar
steps: 1. Carefully place a raw egg inside a cup.
2. Cover the egg completely with vinegar.
3. Let the egg sit for 2 to 3 days, without stirring.
4. Carefully take out the egg and feel how the shell is gone, leaving a "rubbery" egg.
whyItWorks: Vinegar is an acid that slowly dissolves the calcium carbonate in the eggshell, leaving only the thin membrane underneath.
imageAlt: An egg with its shell removed after sitting in vinegar, showing the membrane

title: Sink or float?
materials: Various small household objects (coin, cork, button, leaf, eraser, plastic lid)
steps: 1. Fill a basin with water.
2. Before testing each object, guess whether it will float or sink.
3. Place each object in the water, one at a time, and watch what happens.
4. Sort the objects into two groups: "floats" and "sinks".
whyItWorks: An object floats when it is less dense than water and sinks when it is denser than it.
imageAlt: Several small objects, some floating and some sunk in a basin of water

title: Homemade compass
steps: 1. Rub the needle on a magnet always in the same direction, 20 to 30 times.
2. Carefully push the needle through a cork or piece of foam.
3. Float the cork in the middle of a bowl of water.
4. Watch the needle turn on its own until it always points in the same direction.
whyItWorks: Rubbing the needle on the magnet turns it into a small magnet, which aligns with Earth's magnetic field, always pointing north and south.

title: Red cabbage indicator
steps: 1. Ask an adult to chop the red cabbage into small pieces and cover them with hot water.
2. Wait 15 minutes until the water turns purple, then strain it into a container.
3. Pour a little of the purple liquid into two separate cups.
4. Add vinegar to one cup and baking soda to the other, and watch the colors change.
whyItWorks: Red cabbage juice changes color depending on whether the liquid is acidic (like vinegar, it turns pink) or basic (like baking soda, it turns green or blue).
imageAlt: Cups with red cabbage liquid changing color with vinegar and baking soda

title: Rubber band cardboard car
steps: 1. Tape two straws under the cardboard box, one at the front and one at the back.
2. Push a thin stick through the middle of each bottle cap and slide it into the straws to make the wheels.
3. Stretch a rubber band between the front and back of the box, around one of the axles.
4. Wind up the axle to twist the rubber band, put the car on the ground and let go so it rolls forward on its own.
whyItWorks: The twisted rubber band stores elastic energy, which is released as it untwists and spins the wheels, pushing the car forward.
